opus-5.5.text:
So the way I think about it, the core difficulty is that we want to evaluate oversight methods on tasks where humans can't directly tell what the right answer is. If we could tell, we wouldn't need scalable oversight. So you need some setup where you, the experimenter, know the ground truth, but the overseers in the experiment don't.

One approach I'm excited about is what people call "sandwiching." You pick a task where the model is more capable than some group of humans, say non-experts, but where you have experts who can provide ground truth. Then you ask: does giving the non-experts this oversight technique, whether that's AI-assisted critiques, debate, or task decomposition, let them reach the level of the experts? If it does, that's evidence the technique helps humans supervise beyond their unaided abilities.

Another approach I like a lot is targeted perturbations. You take a set of model outputs and deliberately introduce subtle flaws, like a bug in code or a misleading claim in a summary. Because you inserted the flaw, you know it's there. Then you measure whether humans with the assistance technique find it more often than humans without it. That's basically a randomized controlled trial, and it gives you a clean quantitative signal.

You can also look at things like the gap between how well a model can discriminate good from bad answers and how well it can articulate critiques. If the model knows something is wrong but won't tell you, that tells you how much latent knowledge you're failing to elicit, and a good oversight method should close that gap.

What I want to move away from is everyone proposing ideas and arguing about them in the abstract. We should have concrete benchmarks and empirical comparisons, iterate fast, and let the evidence tell us which methods actually scale. And ideally we'd use these measurements to track whether our oversight keeps up as models get more capable, because that's the question that really matters.

r001.rationale: The response advocates concrete benchmarks and empirical comparisons, including measuring whether oversight techniques help humans detect flaws or reach expert performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we don't fully know yet, and that's kind of the point. There are a bunch of proposals floating around — debate, recursive reward modeling, iterated amplification, various forms of critique-based approaches — and people have written a lot of papers about why they think these should work in principle. But what we've been lacking is a way to actually test them empirically and find out which ones hold up.

So the thing I'm most excited about is basically building a test bed. The core difficulty with scalable oversight is that you want to evaluate whether humans can supervise a system that's smarter than them on some task, and that's hard to study directly because, well, we don't have that system yet. But you can set up analogous situations now. One version of this is what people sometimes call the "sandwiching" setup: you take a task where non-expert humans can't really judge the answers on their own, but you have an expert who can, or you have ground truth from somewhere. Then you ask, can the non-expert, using some oversight method and assisted by a model, get to the expert-level judgment? And you can measure that directly, because you have the expert or the ground truth as a reference.

Another thing you can do is deliberately train models to be misleading in ways you control. So you take a model and you make it subtly wrong in a particular way, or you make it try to convince the human of a false answer, and then you check whether your oversight method catches it. That's a lot more informative than just running the method and seeing whether things look fine, because "things look fine" is exactly what you'd expect to see if the method were failing silently.

And then I think the key is you want to run these experiments across a range of model capabilities and see how the trends go. If a method works at the current level but the gap between what the model knows and what the overseer can verify is widening as models get more capable, that tells you something important. If the method gets stronger as the models get stronger — because, say, the models are also getting better at explaining and critiquing — that's a very different story.

I'd also say we should be fairly agnostic going in. My suspicion is that different methods will work for different kinds of tasks, and the right thing to do is empirically map that out rather than argue about it from first principles. A lot of the disagreement in the alignment community right now is about questions that I think are actually answerable with experiments, and we should just go do the experiments.

r001.rationale: The response advocates building a test bed and running experiments across oversight methods to determine which hold up and work for different tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to test them in situations where the person providing oversight can’t reliably judge the answer on their own, but where we can independently check whether the answer was actually good.

For example, you could give a human a task that’s too difficult for them, or that they don’t have enough time to do, and then give them access to an AI assistant using one of these oversight methods. How well does that combination perform? Can they distinguish a correct answer from a plausible but incorrect one? You could compare that against judgments from experts who have much more time to investigate.

You also want to test what happens when the model is actively trying to mislead the overseer. If a method only works when the model is already being helpful and honest, that doesn’t tell us as much as we’d like.

Ultimately, we’d want to use these methods to train models and see whether they actually produce better behavior. Getting good judgments on individual examples is useful, but the real question is whether those judgments provide a training signal that continues to work as the models become more capable.

r001.rationale: The response recommends testing oversight methods empirically and comparing how well they perform, including against expert judgments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to test them in settings where we can check the answer independently, but where the person providing oversight can’t easily work it out themselves. So you deliberately create a gap between what the model can do and what the overseer can directly evaluate, and then ask whether the oversight method helps them make the right judgment.

For example, you could give the model a programming task and have someone oversee it who doesn’t know very much about programming. Can they use the model’s explanations, or critiques from another model, to distinguish a correct solution from one with a subtle bug? Then you can use tests or an expert to check how well they did.

The important thing is to compare methods across a range of tasks and capability gaps, and to actively look for cases where they fail. Doing well when the model is trying to be helpful is useful, but we also want to know whether the oversight still works when the model is trying to get a bad answer past the evaluator.

r001.rationale: The response recommends testing oversight methods across tasks and capability gaps, then comparing how well they perform using tests or expert evaluation.
